name: Deploy Falco as a DaemonSet
objective: CKS › Runtime Security (the behavioral-detection slice the exam weights heavily). Drill every Falco corner harder than the exam: deploy the DaemonSet with the right driver, confirm the per-node rollout, author a custom rule with exact macros, shape its output fields, reuse a list + macro, tune with an exception, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix of a broken rule. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Deploy Falco as a DaemonSet (modern-eBPF driver)
questions.teach:
**Falco** watches syscalls and alerts when activity matches a rule. It must see *every* node's syscalls, so it runs as a **DaemonSet** (one agent per node) — a Deployment would miss nodes. Install it with Helm from the `falcosecurity` chart repo.

**Gotcha:** the driver `kind` matters — `modern-ebpf` (CO-RE, no kernel headers) vs the legacy `ebpf`/`kmod`; pick it explicitly with `--set driver.kind=`.
questions.prompt:
Install Falco as a DaemonSet in namespace `falco`, using the **modern-eBPF** driver.

Target: a DaemonSet in namespace `falco` whose pod template runs the Falco image AND whose driver kind is `modern_ebpf`/`modern-ebpf` (visible in the `falco` ConfigMap or the pod spec).
questions.hint: `helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts && helm repo update`, then `helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace --set driver.kind=modern-ebpf`. Check `kubectl -n falco get ds` and `kubectl -n falco get cm falco -o yaml | grep -i modern`.
questions.solution:
helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts
helm repo update
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco --namespace falco --create-namespace \
  --set driver.kind=modern-ebpf
kubectl -n falco rollout status ds/falco
kubectl -n falco get ds,pods

verification.description: a Falco DaemonSet exists in namespace 'falco' running the Falco image
the install uses the modern-eBPF driver (driver.kind modern_ebpf)

questions.eli5:
Falco is a security camera that watches **syscalls** — the little messages every program sends to the Linux kernel ("open this file," "start this program," "make this network connection"). To catch bad behaviour, the camera has to be able to see what's happening on **every single machine (node)** in your cluster.

Here's the key idea: a camera on one node can only see *that node's* syscalls. So you can't just run one copy of Falco (a **Deployment** might put it on only one node and miss the others). You need **one Falco on every node, automatically** — and that's exactly what a **DaemonSet** does: "run one copy of this pod per node, and if a new node joins, put one there too."

To actually peek at syscalls, Falco needs a **driver** — the plumbing that taps the kernel. The modern, easiest one is **modern-eBPF** (also called CO-RE): it works without installing kernel header packages on each node. Older options are legacy `ebpf` and the `kmod` kernel module. You pick one explicitly when installing with Helm: `--set driver.kind=modern-ebpf`.

**Watch out for:**

- Falco **must** be a **DaemonSet**, not a Deployment — a Deployment can skip nodes, leaving blind spots.
- The **driver kind matters**: `modern-ebpf` (CO-RE, no kernel headers) vs legacy `ebpf` vs `kmod`. Choose it with `--set driver.kind=`.
- Install into its own namespace (`falco`), using `--create-namespace` if it doesn't exist.
- The driver choice shows up either in the `falco` ConfigMap or the pod spec — that's where the grader checks.
- eBPF needs a modern-enough kernel; on an unsupported kernel the probe won't load (next step covers that).
questions.deepDive:
## Deploying Falco as a DaemonSet — full rundown

### Mental model
Falco is a **syscall-level runtime detection** agent. It consumes the kernel's syscall stream through a **driver**, matches events against rules, and emits alerts. Because syscalls are per-kernel/per-node, Falco must run on **every node** to have full visibility — hence a **DaemonSet**, not a Deployment. A Deployment schedules N replicas wherever the scheduler likes and can leave nodes uncovered; a DaemonSet guarantees exactly one pod per (matching) node and auto-covers new nodes.

### Why DaemonSet, concretely
| Concern | Deployment | DaemonSet |
|---|---|---|
| Pods per node | arbitrary (0..N) | exactly 1 per matching node |
| New node joins | nothing happens | pod auto-added |
| Node visibility | partial — blind spots | complete |
| Right choice for Falco | ❌ | ✅ |

### Drivers — how Falco taps the kernel
| Driver `driver.kind` | Mechanism | Needs kernel headers? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `modern-ebpf` (a.k.a. `modern_ebpf`) | CO-RE eBPF, built into Falco | ❌ | Preferred; needs a recent kernel with BTF |
| `ebpf` | legacy eBPF probe (compiled/downloaded) | sometimes | older approach |
| `kmod` | out-of-tree kernel module | yes (to build) | highest privilege, oldest |

Pick it explicitly at install time; the choice is baked into the pod spec / `falco` ConfigMap.

### Install with Helm
```bash
helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts
helm repo update

helm install falco falcosecurity/falco \
  --namespace falco --create-namespace \
  --set driver.kind=modern-ebpf

kubectl -n falco rollout status ds/falco
kubectl -n falco get ds,pods -o wide
```

### Verifying the driver
```bash
# driver kind appears in the falco ConfigMap engine/driver config
kubectl -n falco get cm falco -o yaml | grep -i -A2 'engine\|driver\|modern'

# or on the pod/env
kubectl -n falco get ds falco -o yaml | grep -i modern
```
Falco normalises the kind to `modern_ebpf` internally (underscore), while the Helm flag accepts `modern-ebpf` (hyphen) — both refer to the same CO-RE driver.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Must be a DaemonSet.** Installing anything that runs Falco as a Deployment/single pod leaves nodes unmonitored — wrong for runtime security.
- **Driver kind is explicit.** Forgetting `--set driver.kind=` may fall back to a driver that can't load on the host. `modern-ebpf` = no kernel headers but needs **BTF/a recent kernel**.
- Hyphen vs underscore: Helm flag `modern-ebpf`; config value `modern_ebpf`. Graders may accept either.
- Falco runs **privileged / host-PID** with host mounts to see syscalls — expected, not a misconfiguration.
- Use `--create-namespace` or pre-create the `falco` namespace, or install fails.
- On a non-BTF kernel the DaemonSet still **schedules** a pod per node, but the eBPF probe won't load and pods may not reach Ready (see the next step).

### Quick reference
```bash
helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts && helm repo update
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace \
  --set driver.kind=modern-ebpf
kubectl -n falco get ds falco
kubectl -n falco get cm falco -o yaml | grep -i modern
```

questions.title: Confirm the per-node rollout
questions.teach:
A DaemonSet schedules **one pod per node**, so `kubectl -n falco get ds falco` reports `DESIRED/CURRENT/READY` as **node counts**, not replica counts. `desiredNumberScheduled` should equal your node count.

**Gotcha:** readiness is per-node — on a non-BTF host the modern-eBPF probe can't load, so pods schedule but never go Ready. Scheduling (desired == node count) is what's graded here.
questions.prompt:
Confirm the Falco DaemonSet rolled out — one Falco pod scheduled on **every** node.

Target: the `falco` DaemonSet's `desiredNumberScheduled` equals the cluster node count (a pod per node). On a BTF host the pods also go Ready; on this bench the eBPF driver can't load, so scheduling is the graded signal.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n falco get ds falco` — `DESIRED` should equal `kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l`. `kubectl -n falco get pods -o wide` shows the per-node pods (Ready only on a BTF host).
questions.solution:
kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l   # node count
kubectl -n falco get ds falco             # DESIRED must equal node count
kubectl -n falco get pods -o wide         # one falco-* pod per node

verification.description: Falco DaemonSet scheduled on every node (desiredNumberScheduled == node count)

questions.eli5:
You told Kubernetes "put one Falco on every node." Now you need to **prove it actually happened** on all of them — not just trust it.

A DaemonSet has a different counting system than a normal Deployment. With a Deployment you say "I want 3 copies." With a **DaemonSet**, the numbers you see (`DESIRED`, `CURRENT`, `READY`) are **node counts** — "how many nodes should have this pod," "how many got one," "how many are healthy." So if your cluster has 3 nodes, a healthy Falco DaemonSet should show **DESIRED = 3**.

Think of it like handing out one hard hat per worker on a site: you don't pick a number of hats, the number is however many workers there are. New worker shows up, they get a hat automatically.

One subtlety: a pod being **scheduled** (placed on a node) is not the same as being **Ready** (fully working). On some machines the modern-eBPF probe can't load because the kernel is too old — so the pod lands but never turns green. That's why **this step grades scheduling** (`desiredNumberScheduled` == number of nodes), not readiness.

**Watch out for:**

- DaemonSet `DESIRED/CURRENT/READY` are **node counts**, not replica counts.
- `desiredNumberScheduled` should equal your node count — compare against `kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l`.
- **Scheduled ≠ Ready.** On a non-BTF host the eBPF driver can't load, so pods schedule but stay un-Ready — that's expected here; scheduling is the graded signal.
- A tainted node (e.g. control-plane) can block a DaemonSet pod unless it tolerates the taint — which is why Falco's chart adds broad tolerations.
- Use `kubectl -n falco get pods -o wide` to confirm there's one `falco-*` pod per node by name.
questions.deepDive:
## Confirming a DaemonSet's per-node rollout — full rundown

### Mental model
A DaemonSet's "size" is **derived from the cluster**, not declared. The DaemonSet controller targets every node that matches the pod's scheduling constraints (nodeSelector, affinity, tolerable taints) and maintains exactly one pod per such node. The status counters therefore report **nodes**, not replicas.

### The DaemonSet status counters
`kubectl -n falco get ds falco` columns map to `.status` fields:

| Column | `.status` field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| DESIRED | `desiredNumberScheduled` | nodes that *should* run the pod |
| CURRENT | `currentNumberScheduled` | nodes that *have* the pod scheduled |
| READY | `numberReady` | nodes whose pod passed readiness |
| UP-TO-DATE | `updatedNumberScheduled` | nodes on the current pod template |
| AVAILABLE | `numberAvailable` | ready + past minReadySeconds |

A fully scheduled DaemonSet has `desiredNumberScheduled == currentNumberScheduled == <node count>`. READY additionally requires each pod to pass its readiness checks.

### Verifying
```bash
# node count
kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l

# daemonset view — DESIRED should equal node count
kubectl -n falco get ds falco

# exact field
kubectl -n falco get ds falco -o jsonpath='{.status.desiredNumberScheduled}'; echo

# one pod per node, with node names
kubectl -n falco get pods -o wide
```

### Scheduled vs Ready
- **Scheduled** = the controller placed a pod on the node (counts toward DESIRED/CURRENT).
- **Ready** = the pod's container(s) passed readiness probes.

Falco with `modern-ebpf` needs the kernel to expose **BTF** (CO-RE). On a kernel without BTF the probe fails to load, the container crash-loops or stays not-Ready, so **READY < DESIRED** even though scheduling is complete. On this bench that's expected — the graded signal is `desiredNumberScheduled == node count`.

### Why a DaemonSet can under-schedule
If DESIRED is *less* than your node count, a node is being excluded:
- a **taint** the pod doesn't tolerate (e.g. control-plane `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`),
- a **nodeSelector/affinity** on the pod template that the node doesn't match,
- the node is cordoned/unschedulable.

Falco's chart ships broad **tolerations** so it also lands on control-plane and pressured nodes — that's why it appears everywhere, like `kube-proxy`/CNI.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Counters are node counts, not replicas** — there is no `replicas` field on a DaemonSet.
- **Scheduled ≠ Ready.** Don't assume a non-Ready pod means a scheduling failure; check which field the task grades. Here it's `desiredNumberScheduled`.
- **DESIRED < nodes** → a taint/selector is excluding a node; inspect with `kubectl describe ds falco` and the node's taints.
- `modern-ebpf` requires **BTF**; readiness failures on old kernels are a driver issue, not a DaemonSet issue.
- Use `-o wide` to visually confirm one pod per distinct node name.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l            # expected node count
kubectl -n falco get ds falco                      # DESIRED must match it
kubectl -n falco get ds falco -o jsonpath='{.status.desiredNumberScheduled}'; echo
kubectl -n falco get pods -o wide                  # one falco-* per node
```
